A.explanation: Both $R_X$ and $R_Y$ increase, so the fraction $R_X/(R_X+R_Y)$ can increase, decrease or stay the same depending on the relative sizes of the changes.

B.explanation: A larger $R_X$ takes a larger share of the fixed battery e.m.f. while a smaller $R_Y$ takes a smaller share, so $V_X$ must increase.

C.explanation: A smaller $R_X$ takes a smaller share and a larger $R_Y$ takes a larger share, so $V_X$ must decrease.

D.explanation: Both $R_X$ and $R_Y$ decrease, so the fraction $R_X/(R_X+R_Y)$ can increase, decrease or stay the same depending on the relative sizes of the changes.

hints: Notice that $V_X$ is the p.d. across $R_X$ in a series loop with $R_Y$ and a battery of fixed e.m.f., so the two resistors share the total p.d.
Recall the potential divider rule $V_X = V \times R_X/(R_X+R_Y)$, which can also be written as $V_X = V/(1+R_Y/R_X)$.
Ask what happens to the ratio $R_Y/R_X$ when $R_X$ gets larger at the same time as $R_Y$ gets smaller, and what that does to $V_X$.
walkthrough: Identify the circuit: $R_X$ and $R_Y$ are in series across a battery of constant e.m.f. $V$, with negligible internal resistance, so $V_X + V_Y = V$.
State the divider rule: current $I = V/(R_X+R_Y)$ is common, so $V_X = I R_X = V \times R_X/(R_X+R_Y)$.
Rewrite to show the competition clearly: $V_X = V/(1+R_Y/R_X)$, so $V_X$ increases whenever the ratio $R_Y/R_X$ decreases.
If $R_X$ is made larger the numerator of $R_X/(R_X+R_Y)$ grows, and if $R_Y$ is made smaller the denominator grows less, so the fraction must grow.
If both change in the same direction the result is uncertain because the fraction depends on which change dominates, and opposite changes in the other sense must lower $V_X$.
Therefore larger $R_X$ combined with smaller $R_Y$ must cause $V_X$ to increase. This is option B.
